findings.passage: Yet in a decade of interviews about the films that went wrong, she has never described a set as a place where she was misled or left unprotected.
findings.problem: This absolute is the hinge of the discriminator, and it is repeated in FAQ 2 ("never that she was misled or left unprotected") and compressed into the meta description. The frozen record does not support "never." (a) C165's own context is that James scrapped Patrick Marber's script after Johnson signed; the record's inference reads her "it was scary" as fear "of being bound by contract to a production that had changed under her," which is a production changing after she committed, the shape the article says a Six's injury takes. The body presents the fear as "a contract at 23" with no mention of the script change. (b) C136 is trimmed: the draft quotes "It would've been like, 'Oh, this is psychotic.' But no, I don't regret it," and drops the lead-in "If I had known at the time that's what it was going to be like, I don't think anyone would've done it," the most misled-shaped sentence in the record. (c) S45 (opened by me on 2026-10-08): "I can't waste time on toxic sets anymore, or in situations that are not fun or fulfilling or healthy," defined as sets with "anybody who's mean or condescending or unkind." It is first-person testimony to having worked on sets she calls unhealthy, it is not in the claim inventory, and it is not in the draft. (d) "In a movie like that, I have no say about anything" (C28) is a powerlessness complaint the body quotes elsewhere. A fair reading may still find that none of these names a person who betrayed her, but the article has to say that with these lines on the page, not by omitting them.
findings.acceptance_test: The body quotes the Marber-script context beside "I was 23. So it was scary," restores "If I had known at the time that's what it was going to be like, I don't think anyone would've done it" where the regret line appears, adds the S45 "toxic sets" line (with its unkindness definition) to the inventory and the body, and then either argues why these still fit a grievance about the work or replaces "never described a set as a place where she was misled or left unprotected" with a bounded claim (e.g. she has not named anyone who misled her, and the fear she attaches to Fifty Shades is of a production that changed after she signed). FAQ 2 and the meta description are changed to match. Total words stay under 4,500 by cutting elsewhere.

findings.passage: Even the "shepherd" trust rested on being seen: she trusted Gyllenhaal "because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen."
findings.problem: The S03 sentence continues: "She knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care." The draft cuts the half that is protection-and-care language (the Six reading's vocabulary) and then asserts that the trust "rested on being seen." The record's own C100 alternative flags exactly this. In the paragraph where the article claims her self-definition and her trust share one content, a quote has been trimmed to make that true.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence quotes both halves ("not be seen" and "not be handled with grace and with care") and the claim about what the trust rested on is rewritten to acknowledge that she named being seen and being handled with care together; C100's passage is updated to the full quotation.

findings.passage: Six theory predicts fear managed through preparation, allies and authority; Four theory predicts fear tolerated for the sake of feeling and being seen. Her stated overrides fit the second.
findings.problem: The overrides the draft itself quotes run through allies first. Burghardt: "I don't have the confidence, but, with her, I feel very protective and I know her very well" precedes "I can see this world" in one continuous quote (S45, confirmed). Gyllenhaal is her "shepherd." On Materialists she relaxed because she was "in such good hands." The 2023 low day ended when her partner noticed. "When I feel safe, I think I can do anything." That is the ally mechanism the sentence assigns to Six theory, present in the same breath as the vision claims. "Her stated overrides fit the second" is therefore not what the evidence shows; both mechanisms appear together, and the Four tilt can only rest on what she adds (vision, curiosity, exposure), not on the absence of allies.
findings.acceptance_test: The clean dichotomy is replaced by a sentence stating that her overrides contain both a trusted person and a vision or exposure claim, usually in the same answer, and that the article's tilt toward Four rests on the content she adds rather than on the absence of ally-seeking; or the paragraph's concluding claim is cut.

findings.passage: Two independent accounts describe that fight as a clash of visions, Taylor-Johnson's "Her vision versus mine" and James's "I had to fight for a lot of things really hard," rather than a betrayal.
findings.problem: Taylor-Johnson is describing her own dispute with James; James is describing her advocacy for readers, days before the film opened and years before anyone complained. Neither says anything about how Johnson experienced the production, so neither can establish that Johnson's grievance was "a clash of visions rather than a betrayal." The draft concedes this itself later ("neither speaks to her motives"), then uses them here as if they settled the shape of her injury. Presented inside the discriminator paragraph, this reads as independent corroboration that the Six story is excluded, which the sources cannot provide.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence is limited to what the two accounts show (that the creative-control fight on the first film existed and was two-sided) and the characterization of Johnson's own grievance as vision rather than betrayal is attributed only to her words (C184), with the later "neither speaks to her motives" sentence left intact.

findings.passage: Against it, she keeps puncturing her own image where winning happens: she doesn't "make sense" in the superhero world, shrugs at "tiny movies that didn't do well," and would accept a small Italian film as her last.
findings.problem: The Three rebuttal omits the adverse lines sitting next to the ones it uses. In the LA Times exchange (S06, opened 2026-10-08), the first words out of her mouth on Madame Web are "It wasn't my fault," said laughing, followed by decisions "made by committee" and "by people who don't have a creative bone in their body," then "along for the ride," then "Who cares?" The draft keeps the shrug and drops the disclaimer. "I don't make sense in that world" was an answer to a question about nasty reviews, given weeks after the flop; that is as naturally read as distancing from a failure as puncturing an image. And the 2022 unburdening about Fifty Shades came after the franchise ended (2018) and after her prestige turn in The Lost Daughter (2021), the moment when distancing is cheapest; the one-clause dismissal ("fit that story poorly") never engages the timing. The record ranks Three the second rival; the body gives it a rebuttal that only works because the blame-deflecting half of the evidence is absent.
findings.acceptance_test: "It wasn't my fault" (with its laughing delivery and the committee line) is added to the inventory and quoted in the Three paragraph; the timing of the 2022 account relative to the franchise's end and The Lost Daughter is stated; the paragraph then names a discriminator against Three that survives those lines (for example the content of what she wants when nothing is at stake) or concedes that the Three reading is less settled than written.

findings.passage: Her industry critique keeps that shape.
findings.problem: The section presents only the Four-shaped lines of her industry critique. From the same L'Officiel answer as "the safe thing is really boring" the draft omits "The people who run streaming platforms don't trust creative people or artists to know what's going to work" (C179), which the research record itself flags as the line that lets the critique be read as distrust of authority (Six). It also omits Cannes's "It's a constant fight. But we are fighters" (C187) while using "fighters" in the persona title. Adverse framing that the record identified is left out of the body.
findings.acceptance_test: The "don't trust creative people or artists" line appears beside the "safe thing is really boring" line with one sentence saying why it fits a distrust reading and why the draft still reads her stated remedy as difference; C179's passage is updated.

findings.passage: Not that she was good, or that she had arrived. That she did something different.
findings.problem: The gloss reads only the word "different." The compliment came from David Fincher, one of the most exacting directors working, about a role he said "could have easily been thankless"; treasuring praise from the hardest authority in the room is also what a Six (validation from a trusted authority) or a Three (recognition from the best) would treasure most. The draft's confident two-sentence reading presents one of three available readings as the only one.
findings.acceptance_test: The gloss acknowledges who the praise came from and that an authority's approval would be prized by other types, and states that the word she repeated ("different") is what tilts the remark, or the gloss is softened to "this suggests" language.

findings.passage: She prizes chosen family over "the people you're actually born to."
findings.problem: C23 records her explaining what a proverb means ("which means that the connections with people you choose are more solid..."), in an exchange about her blended family where she also says of her half-siblings "I love those kids like my life depends on it." The record does not show her adopting the proverb as her own ranking of chosen over born family; the draft states a definition as a personal value. It is used for the Six case, so the error does not favor the thesis, but it is still an inference presented as fact and may invert her point.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence attributes the definition to her explanation of the saying and either shows from S04 that she endorsed it as her own view or drops the word "prizes" for an accurate paraphrase.

protected_passages.passage: "I found myself as an actor, a few times, showing up to the premiere of a movie to see it the first time," she said. Her verdict on those nights: "That is not what I thought we were making."
protected_passages.reason: A specific, dated, sourced opening that the body actually pays off; the article's best hook.

protected_passages.passage: Still, on her talk of fear and safety alone, the Six reading would win.
protected_passages.reason: The concession that keeps the Six case from being token; any repair of the discriminator must leave this standing.

protected_passages.passage: She held a promotional line that was not the whole truth, but the feeling she stated then, pride in something "different," is the one she repeated in 2022. What she withheld was the fight.
protected_passages.reason: A careful, dated reading of the promotional years that separates withholding from faking without overclaiming.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven's appetite usually runs from that sentence. Hers runs toward it.
protected_passages.reason: Distinctive and earned by the adjacent quotation; the clearest single line of type reasoning in the piece.

protected_passages.passage: Even the confession is a bit, and it changes between tellings.
protected_passages.reason: Keeps the limes from being overread while still making the observation that matters.

assessment: Critic read of the frozen draft and evidence (hashes verified). The draft confronts the Six case more honestly than most profiles: a full section, a concession that on fear and safety alone Six would win, and a limits paragraph. The problem is where the discriminator is built. The section that carries the thesis repeatedly keeps the Four-shaped half of a quotation and drops the Six-shaped half from the same sentence or exchange (Gyllenhaal's "grace and with care," the "If I had known" lead-in, Burghardt's "with her... I know her very well"), leaves out lines from opened sources that bear directly on the lede's "never misled or left unprotected" absolute (the Marber-script change after she signed, which the record's own C165 inference describes; "toxic sets" in S45; "It wasn't my fault" in S06, both confirmed by opening them on 2026-10-08), and uses two outside accounts of a different dispute as if they characterized hers. The Three rebuttal works only because the blame-deflecting line next to the shrug is absent. The Four reading may still lead on content once these lines are on the page; what cannot stand is the absolute in the lede, FAQ 2 and the meta description. Smaller notes for the editor, not findings: the Bustle "exaggerated" caveat is placed directly after the Six's sharpest line and not restated where Bustle supports Four, which reads as asymmetric discounting; and S45 also has her saying of sets "It's not a fight. It's not a race. It's a collaboration," which sits oddly beside the persona title "The Tender Fighter" and the Cannes "we are fighters." Similarity diagnostic: every tripped pair is this subject's own earlier draft (the same argument, revised), not another profile; the highest cross-subject score (0.053, Jeremy Allen White) is a sentence shape ("X cannot settle Y"), not a reused argument; limitation: only five diagnosis units were compared. Draft is 4,297 words, so every addition requested above must displace something.
